en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Rattandhakāravagga 15.
The Training Rule on Departing Without Asking Permission.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhunī was a regular visitor to a certain family, receiving a fixed meal there.
Then, having dressed in the morning and taken her bowl and robe, that bhikkhunī approached that family; having approached and sat down on a seat, she departed without informing the owners.
While a female slave of that family was sweeping the house, she tucked that seat away among the utensils.
People, not seeing that seat, said this to the bhikkhunī:
“Where is that seat, noble lady?
“I do not see that seat, friends,” she replied.
“Go away, venerable lady! This seat is for you! Having reviled her thus, they cut off her regular meal.
Then, while those people were cleaning their house, they saw that seat among the gaps between the vessels; they asked that bhikkhunī for forgiveness and established a regular meal for her once again.
Then that bhikkhunī reported this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can a bhikkhunī, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, depart without having asked permission from the master? ... [The Buddha asked:
"Is it true, monks, that a bhikkhunī, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, departs without having asked permission from the master?"

“It is true, Blessed One. The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them: “… How indeed, monks, can a nun, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, depart without having asked permission from the owners? This is not for the benefit of unbelievers, nor for the increase of those who have faith…” [as in the standard formula]. He addressed the bhikkhunīs: “Nuns, a rule of training should be laid down thus: ‘A nun who, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, departs without having asked permission from the owners, is guilty of an offense of wrong-doing. Thus was this rule of training laid down by the Blessed One. Now at that time, a certain nun was ill. She thought: “The Blessed One has laid down a rule of training: ‘A nun who, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, departs without having asked permission from the owners, is guilty of an offense of wrong-doing. What if I were to sit right here until the meal is finished? She sat there until the meal was finished. The people became annoyed, irritated, and indignant, saying: “How can these nuns sit and eat as if they were the masters of the house? They complained and criticized them to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Monks, a nun who is ill may sit on a seat in a family before the meal and remain there until the meal is finished. But a nun who is not ill, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, must not depart without having asked permission from the owners. Whoever should so depart is guilty of an offense of wrong-doing. Thus was this rule of training laid down by the Blessed One. Now at that time, a certain nun was going to the village for alms. She thought: “The Blessed One has laid down a rule of training: ‘A nun who, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, must not depart without having asked permission from the owners. What if I were to ask permission from the owners when I am about to leave? She asked permission from the owners when she was about to leave. The people became annoyed, irritated, and indignant, saying: “How can these nuns act as if they were the mistresses of the household? They complained and criticized them to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Monks, a nun who is going to the village for alms, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, may depart without asking permission from the owners. But a nun who is not going to the village for alms, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, must not depart without having asked permission from the owners. Whoever should so depart is guilty of an offense of wrong-doing. Thus was this rule of training laid down by the Blessed One. Now at that time, a certain nun was going to the village for alms. She thought: “The Blessed One has laid down a rule of training: ‘A nun who, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, must not depart without having asked permission from the owners. What if I were to ask permission from the owners when I have already left? She asked permission from the owners after she had already left. “Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule thus:
‘If any nun, having approached families before the meal and sat down on a seat, should depart without having informed the owner, it is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya).’”
"But whichever" means whichever such...
"nun" means... [as before].
...pe... this is the nun intended in this context.
"Before the meal" means from the rising of the sun until midday.
"Family" means four families: the khattiya family, the brahmin family, the vessa family, and the sudda family.
"Having approached" means...
Having gone there:
"seat" (āsana) refers to the space for a couch (pallaṅka).
"Having sat down" means having sat down on that [seat].
"Should depart without asking the owner" means: [as stated above].
If she passes beyond the sheltered area without having asked permission from the wise person in that family, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she passes beyond the precincts in the open air, it is an offense of expiation.
If she has not asked for permission and perceives that she has not asked for permission, yet she departs, it is an offense of expiation.
If she departs without having asked for permission while being in doubt, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she departs without having asked for permission while perceiving that she has asked for permission, there is an offense of expiation.
If it is not the proper place for a couch, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one has asked for permission, but perceives that one has not asked for permission, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one has asked for permission, but is in doubt about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one has asked for permission and perceives that one has asked for permission, there is no offense.
There is no offense if she goes after having asked for permission,
or if the items are not portable.
For one who is ill,
in cases of emergency,
for one who is insane,
"By one who is a first-offender":
thus ends the fifth training rule.
